title: The object exists independent of the mind (4.14–4.17)
hook: one photo, two colors, and a very old answer about what's really there

segments.voice: Yesterday: vasana, the trace of desire with no beginning, which still fades when its supports are gone.

In 2015, a photo of a dress split the internet. Half the people saw blue and black. The other half saw white and gold, and couldn't believe anyone saw anything else. Families argued at dinner. Same photo, same screen, two different dresses. It's an old question in a new outfit: if two minds see one thing so differently, is there really one thing there? Or does each mind make its own world? Patanjali takes that on directly, and he picks a side.
screen: `ONE PHOTO, TWO DRESSES.` → `IS THERE ONE THING THERE AT ALL?` → `PATANJALI PICKS A SIDE.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.15: vastusamye chittabhedat tayor vibhaktah panthah. The thing being the same, because the minds differ, the two go separate ways. Vastu is the real object out there; chitta is the mind. One dress, two minds, two paths. Patanjali doesn't conclude the dress is imaginary. The difference is in the minds. Sutra 4.14 had already said a thing has its own reality, from the unity of its changes. The next thread pushes further: an object doesn't depend on any one mind. If it did, what would it be when that mind looked away? Would your kitchen vanish while you sleep? Then 4.17 adds the subtle part. A thing is known or not known depending on whether the mind is colored by it. The object is there either way; knowing it is the mind taking on its color, like a clear glass set on red cloth. Why argue this in a book about freedom? The commentators were in conversation with other thinkers of their day, some of them Buddhist philosophers, who held that what we call objects are constructions of mind. Yoga, with its sister school Samkhya, holds that the world is real. That matters for practice. The problem was never that the world is fake. It's the coloring: the wanting, the dread, the story the mind smears onto the tree outside.
screen: `ONE THING, TWO MINDS, TWO PATHS.` · `IT DOESN'T DEPEND ON ONE MIND.` · `KNOWING IS THE MIND TAKING COLOR.` · `THE WORLD IS REAL; THE COLORING ISN'T.` · then, large: `VASTUSĀMYE CITTABHEDĀT TAYOR VIBHAKTAḤ PANTHĀḤ.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on one ordinary object near you, a cup, a chair, a plant, and notice the colors your mind lays on it: I like this, this needs washing, someone gave me this. Name each one softly and set it aside. Then let the thing just be there, as itself.
Vastu, the real object out there. For Patanjali, the world is real; minds differ in how they are colored by it.
Your line: realism. The world is real; the coloring comes from the mind. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 484 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MIND IS NOT SELF-LUMINOUS.`

howItsDone: Classical Yoga, like Samkhya, is taught as a realist philosophy: the world of nature is real, and practice aims at freeing the mind from the coloring it takes on, not at denying the world.

original.note: Sanskrit vastu: a thing, a real object, something that exists.

trapdoor: what you thought: if everyone sees it differently, nothing is really there.
what it means: the thing is real; minds differ in how it colors them.

what a scholar hears: the Vyasa commentary on 4.14–4.16 argues against the view that objects are only constructions of consciousness, keeping Yoga with Samkhya's realism; some editions treat 4.16 as part of the commentary.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): the teaser called the answer 'two-thousand-year-old'; the Yoga Sutras' date is disputed (estimates run from before the common era to around 400 CE), so it now says 'very old'.
Some editions and scholars treat 4.16 as a line of the commentary rather than a sutra; the script describes it as 'the next thread'. Confirm framing.
The opponents in the commentary are commonly identified as Buddhist idealists (Vijnanavada/Yogacara). Stated descriptively, without ranking; confirm the Keeper is comfortable naming them.
The 2015 'dress' photo is used as an everyday illustration (February 2015).
The clear glass on red cloth echoes the crystal image of Yoga Sutra 1.41; here it is the script's own illustration.
